title_en: Mala and Tilak Given to Gopaldas and Santdas
translation:
Gopaldas and Santdas, both Ramanandi in background, have now been given kanthi diksha (initiation with the sacred neck-thread). Earlier, when Jivanji Maharaj had left Gujarat together with Guru Gopaldas and gone to the house of an acquaintance (melapi) in Malwa, he has now returned to the home of that same close friend of Guru Gopaldas -- Gopaldas of the village of Khediya. Since this Gopaldas is older in age, he is known as elder (Motha) Gopaldas. Jivanji Maharaj, wandering from place to place, has come back here. Meanwhile, a very devout and pious relative of elder Gopaldas had earlier told him that if any true saint should come, he should be introduced. So elder Gopaldas had been waiting for Jivanji Maharaj's return, and today Jivanji Maharaj himself stood at his door. Remembering what his affectionate relative had said, elder Gopaldas takes Jivanji Maharaj along with him to a village named Chanderiya, to bestow grace upon his relative there.

If a true saint could be found in Chanderiya, one's life would be redeemed and one would attain the supreme state -- with this hope sat elder Gopaldas's dear relative, who is also named Gopaldas. Today his wish bore fruit: Jivanji Maharaj has come here. For one who had waited for a true saint the way the chatak bird waits for rain, it felt today as though the first shower of the Shravan monsoon was about to fall. Seeing Jivanji Maharaj, Gopaldas of Chanderiya -- steeped in the flavour of devotion, who had waited with true, heartfelt longing -- says:

_Chanderiye vaase vasu, Jivan pragate aay,
Sitapati Raghunathko, deeno naam bataay ||1||_ (I was residing in the village of Chanderiya when Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj appeared and came to me; he gave me initiation and bestowed on me devotion to the Name of Sitapati Ram. -- 1)

_Takiya teenu bahra, jahaan Sitapatike sant,
Sadguru mile Gopalku, tab paaya naam anant ||2||_ (Takiya = a fixed seat/resolve, beyond the three [worldly attachments], held only toward a true saint devoted to Sitapati Ram, who is beyond the three gunas. Fixing my gaze on such a one alone and settling my resolve there, Gopaldas says that when he met Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj he thereby attained the infinite Name. -- 2)

_Sadguru Jivan umage, shyaam ghata ghan ghor,
Ajhar jhare ras peejiye, so nirakhat jugal kishor ||3||_ (Just as a mass of dark clouds gathers and surges forth joyfully, so has Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj come surging upon me with great love; and now, just as yogis on the path of yoga drink the ajhar-ras -- the nectar that, at a certain advanced stage, flows down from the crown of the head into the mouth, and which they drink with great love -- so I too, gazing upon the Divine Youthful Pair [Radha-Krishna], shall drink a love-devotion nectar even finer than ajhar-ras. -- 3. [Shankarbhai Patel, a farmer of Puniyad village, who himself drank such ajhar-ras, told me of this experience of his. We, however, are capable of experiencing an even finer nectar of love. -- 3.])

_Jab the Jivan pragate, tab the bhayo kalyan,
Raksha bhai Gopalku, ab chumbego jamraan ||4||_ (From the moment Jivanji Maharaj appeared, our welfare has been secured; and now someone like me, Gopaldas, has been given protection from the ocean of worldly existence [bhavsagar]. So the messengers of Yama's abode will strike out in vain -- that is, they will not be able to do anything to me -- and this will vex and grieve them. -- 4)

_Madan jagaayo maanani, saame ven bajaay,
Aise Sadguru Jivana, ham sute liye jagaay ||5||_ (Just as Lord Krishna once played his flute among the honoured, beautiful gopis and awakened Kamdev, the god of love, within them, giving them the nectar of love to drink, so too has Jivanji Maharaj awakened us, who lay asleep in the sleep of delusion [moh-nidra] -- he roused us out of worldly illusion and taught us the path of loving devotion. -- 5)

In Rajasthan, forty kilometres from Bhilwara, there is a railway station on the main road. Next to it is the village of Medi Kheda, one kilometre from the station. Two kilometres further, on the road, is Hajuriya Kheda; and four kilometres from Hajuriya Kheda is the place known as Ramdevji's Chanderiya, or Old (Purana) Chanderiya. Its population is five to seven thousand, made up mainly of Rajput, Jat and other communities. Within three or four kilometres around Chanderiya lie three more villages: Mugaka Kheda, Khir Kheda, and Dagara Kheda. It was into this land that Jivanji Maharaj went to awaken his own devotees (nij-jans), and thereby sanctified this ground.

Having had darshan of Jivanji Maharaj, Gopaldas becomes overjoyed and speaks the sakhis above, in which the feeling of his heart is expressed: that though he dwells in Chanderiya, Jivandasji has come and appeared for his redemption; that the Guru has given him the infinite Name, Ramkabir; and that he is drinking the ajhar-ras of the Guru's word that flows on, and thereby his welfare has been accomplished.

Jivanji Maharaj then answers Gopaldas, in a sakhi, saying --

_Jap tap teerath Jivana, pooja paati prem,
Sant sangat Hari bhajan bin, aur na doojo nem ||6||_ (Jivanji Maharaj says: not japa [mantra repetition], not tapa [austerity], not tirtha [pilgrimage] -- my message and command is this: our worship is not of the vedic ritual kind but pure prem-lakshana [love-natured] devotion; besides keeping the company of saints [satsang] and singing the praises of Hari, we know nothing else, nor do we wish to know anything else -- such is our fixed resolve [tek]. We hold no attachment to reciting mantras, performing austerities, going on pilgrimage, or worshipping with leaves and flowers; the company of saints and devotion to Hari alone is, for us, the rule -- the resolve -- of devotion. -- 6)

In the Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, chapter 196, verses 6-7, it is said that the Vedanta scriptures speak of abandoning the practice of japa, because all their statements are chiefly oriented toward renunciation and the establishment of peace, and culminate only in Brahman -- that is, since japa is itself a form of active engagement (pravritti), it is not the principal means to liberation.

Chapter 197, verse 2, says: men who perform japa (owing to the many distinctions of intellect) fall even into various hells.

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj has given mala and tilak to the devotees of Malwa. It is necessary for us to accept the tulsi kanthi (neck-beads of tulsi wood) and the tilak. Tulsi has eight names:

_Vrinda vrindaavani vishnupoojita vishvapaavani,
Pushpasaara nandini tulasi shreekrishna jeevani ||1||_ (The eight names of Tulsi: Vrinda, Vrindavani, worshipped by Vishnu, purifier of the universe, essence of flowers, Nandini, Tulsi, and the life of Shri Krishna.)

Before making Gopaldas his disciple, Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj had discussed with him the question of Akar-Nirakar (form and formlessness). During that discussion, Gopaldas had, through his own words, explained certain things to Jivanji Maharaj. Now Jivanji Maharaj, in turn, passes on that same teaching, giving mala and tilak to Gopaldas and Santdas of Chanderiya and making them devotees. In doing so he presented again the teaching he himself had received from his own Guru -- and in that teaching came this sakhi of Ranka and Vanka [a devotee couple]. It is presented here once more, so let us understand it again.

Here, mala and tilak were bestowed on both Gopaldas and Santdas, and they accepted Jivanji Maharaj as their Sadguru. Thus Jivanji Maharaj gave mala and tilak to Gopaldas and Santdas; it was through the grace (prataap) of elder Gopaldas (of Khediya) that both of them received the mala and tilak. (7)

Further, through elder Gopaldas, Jivanji Maharaj also gave mala and tilak to Devdas, and spoke this sakhi --

_Dheereku dheeju nahi, aisa paaya naaka,
Aakaar niraakaar vivarjit, taaka sevak Raaka ||7||_ (Ranka Bhagat says: the with-form [sakar] is a worldly, illusory thing, and it is perishable, so I place no trust in it. This is the secret key [naaka -- the device, the insight] my Guru has shown me through his teaching: that the Supreme is the support of all, one who has neither the notion of having form nor of being formless -- I, Ranka Bhagat, am his servant.)

_Dhireku dhiju sahi, rahu adharake maanhi,
Vaanka tahaan vilaambiyaan, jahaan dhoop nahi chhaanya ||2||_ (His wife Vankaji says: this perishable, worldly, with-form body cannot be entirely done away with, for devotion, understanding, spiritual practice, and action all require a body; so I hold to the body only to the extent necessary, but I fix my mind upon the Supreme, who is himself without support yet is the support of all -- my mind has become steady in that. And what is that Supreme like? A place where there is neither the shade nor the sun of the three gunas, no joy, no sorrow, no threefold affliction -- only the very form of supreme bliss.)

While expounding on form and formlessness, [Jivanji Maharaj] gives the example of God assuming the form of Narsingh to protect Prahlad, in order to show God's utterly fierce power. God is all-powerful; were he to will it, he could bring about even the great deluge (mahapralay) -- and the example of God taking the form of Narsingh is given to show this. God's might is shown here through verses of the Narsingh Purana.

Bhairav -- God's Bhairav-like form appeared. Bhairav is a fearsome name of Shiva, of which there are eight or twelve kinds, the chief among them being Kalbhairav. God took on just such a form, described here: at the time of the great deluge, God destroyed -- beginning with Brahma -- the Sun, Indra, the Moon, Kuber, Varun, the wind-god, Mahadev, the fifty-six crore yoginis, sixty-four crore Chamundas, nine crore Katyayanis, endless crores of attendant spirits, and Bhairav and the other forms of Time (Kaal) itself. He seized and drank up that Kaal, and it is for this that Krupanath [the Merciful Lord] bears the name Mahakaal.

The "nine crore Katyayanis" refers to the nine crore forms of Durga, namely: 1. Shailaputri, 2. Brahmacharini, 3. Chandraghanta, 4. Kushmang, 5. Skandhaman, 6. Katyayani, 7. Ratrikal, 8. Mahagauri, and 9. Siddhidatri.

The twelve suns of the twelve months are listed in the Kurma Purana:

Twelve months -- Sun (deity)
Madhu-maas = Chaitra maas -- Dhata
Madhav-maas = Vaishakh maas -- Aryama
Shukra-maas = Jeth maas -- Mitra
Shuchi-maas = Ashadh maas -- Varun
Nabho-maas = Shravan maas -- Indra
Nabhasakhya = Bhadarva maas -- Vishvavan
Tapo-maas = Magh maas -- Pusha
Tapasakhya = Fagan maas -- Parjanya
Saho-maas = Margashirsh -- Anshu
Pushya-maas = Posh maas -- Bhaga
Ishambhara = Aashvin -- Tvashta

There are sixty-four yoginis, who are the attendants of Parvati, and they too have sixty-four names.
There are eight Bhairavs: Asitang, Ruru, Chand, Krodh, Unmatt, Kupati (or Rupali), Bhishan, and Sanhar.

Kabir has sung in the Maru raga --

_(Maru)
Avadhu naade vaade gagan gaajai, sabad anaahad bolai,
Antargate to naahi na dekhai, dhoondhat ban ban dolai. (tek)_ (O renunciant, the sky resounds with sound and music, and the anahad shabd -- the unstruck sound -- keeps sounding on; yet you do not see it within your own inner self, and you wander, searching, from forest to forest.)

_Shaligraam taju Shiv pooja, sir Brahmaka kaatu,
Saayar phodi nirmukta laau, kuvaa sel de paatu ||1||_ (I will give up even the worship of Shaligram and of Shiva; I will cut off the very head of Brahma -- that is, I will not let him go on creating a world of birth and death; I will destroy and do away with the ocean of worldly existence and bring about liberation from bondage.)

_Chandra sooraj doy toobaa kari hai, chit chetanaki daandi,
Sukhamanaa taanti baajan laagi, ih vidh trishnaa khaandi ||2||_ (Into the well of amrit-ras [nectar of immortality] I will lower, with a stroke of love, the rope of my inner awareness [surta]; of that rope I will make the sun and moon its two gourd-floats, and mind and consciousness its crossbar. Thus the strings of the sushumna channel will begin to sound, and in this way I shall quench my thirst for drinking the water of love's nectar.)

_Param tatva aadhaar merai, Shiv nagari ghar meraa,
Kaal hi khaadau michaavi heendun, bahuri na kari hu pheraa ||3||_ (The Supreme Reality, the Paramatma, is my only support, and the city of Shiva is my home, my dwelling place. I shall shatter Time [Kaal] itself and move about fearlessly; no longer shall I go round and round through the cycle of the womb.)

_Japau na jaap hato nahi gugal, pustak lei na padhaau,
Kahai Kabir param pad paayaa, nahi aau nahi jaau ||4||_ (I do not chant japa, nor light incense [gugal], nor take up a book to read. Kabir says: I have attained the supreme state; now I shall neither come nor go -- neither be born nor die.)

Jivanji Maharaj presents this account of Prahlad to show that such fearlessness dwells within a true devotee. Our protector, the Paramatma, is an all-capable being, so there is no need to fear death (Kaal), for our Sadguru has taken us under his shelter, giving us mala, tilak, the company of saints, and the Name of Hari.

Jivanji Maharaj speaks this sakhi and explains the nature of form and formlessness. (We have already seen the exposition of this sakhi earlier, in the chapter on "Morli Manohar Parmeshwar," so it is not repeated here again.) The confusion about form and formlessness is dispelled here as he goes on to explain, giving as evidence the manner in which Prahlad was protected -- God appearing out of a pillar. What kind of pillar was this? The Narsingh Purana describes what form emerged from the burning, red-hot pillar --

_Atiraudram mahaakaayam daanavaanaam bhayankaram,
Mahaanetram mahaavaktram mahaadanshtram mahaabhujam ||32||_ (Extremely terrifying, of huge body, striking fear into the demons; with vast eyes, a vast mouth, vast fangs, and vast arms. -- 32)

_Mahaanakham mahaapaadam kaalaagnisadrishaananam,
Karnaantakritavistaravadanam chaatibheeshanam ||33||_ (With vast claws, vast feet, a face like the fire of universal destruction, eyes stretching to his ears -- utterly dreadful. -- 33)

_Kritvetthan naarasinham tu yayau Vishnustrivikramah,
Narasinha stambhamadhyaad nirgatya prananaad cha ||34||_ (Taking on this terrifying form of Narsingh, Lord Vishnu Trivikram set forth; and this Narsingh, emerging from the middle of the pillar, began to roar fearsomely. -- 34)

(Commentary) The fearsome, Bhairav-like form that appeared from the pillar had endless arms, endless eyes, endless inner faculties, and endless weapons; crores upon crores of flames of fire blazed forth, and one vast, cosmic form (virat swaroop) manifested.

_Kalpaante srishtim sanhatya utkeerya Brahmanonakhaat,
Tvacham shikhaaparyanta abadhnaat mukute prabhuh ||35||_ (At the end of the kalpa [cosmic cycle], having destroyed creation, the Lord flayed the skin of Brahma from his nails to the crown of his head, and bound it into his own crown. -- 35)

_Dvaadashaarkashirohaar Indraadikashirodaamaa,
Yoginichakrabaahookrit traataa Bhairavakaalajit ||36||_ (He wore a garland of the heads of the twelve suns; he made a cord of the heads of Indra and the others; he fashioned arms from the circle of yoginis; and he conquered Bhairav and the other forms of Time. -- 36)

That is: at the end of the deluge he severed (destroyed) the heads of the twelve suns; he destroyed Indra, Som, Kuber, Vayu, and others; he cut off Mahadev's head and bound it to his left foot; the yoginis and others were destroyed; and, having devoured all of these, Krupanath drank up Time (Kaal) itself -- for which he is called Mahakaal. Adhyaruji Maharaj says --

_Kaal tano Mahakaal, Swami paap dahan Gopal,
Tulasi vallabhu e, Hari te surnar durlabh e ||4||_ (Adhyaru 2-10-4-4-4) (He [Parbrahma] is the Kaal of Kaal, that is, Mahakaal; moreover he has the power to burn away anything in the universe, sin included. He is the beloved husband of Tulsi [Vrinda], and he is exceedingly difficult for gods and men alike to understand, know, or attain.)

_Shoorame shooro Shaamalo, Govaale Goval,
Leelaa saluno Jivanaa, Kaal maanhi Mahakaal ||8||_ (Among the brave and mighty, he is the mightiest; among cowherds, he is the finest cowherd; and in his divine play [leela] he is beautiful. Such is Parbrahma -- Mahakaal even among Kaal itself.)

So then -- a thing with form would burn; how then can it be said that he appeared out of that pillar? For the pillar was ablaze, burning red-hot with flames of fire; if he had form he could not have survived, that is, he would have burned. Yet here we say he "appeared" -- so how did he survive? He must, then, be the formless Parbrahma. And if he is formless, then he is as described earlier: he can have no upadhi (identifying attribute) at all -- no great eyes, no great, fearsome teeth, claws, and so on.

We have discussed this subject at length earlier, so there is no need to go over it again here. But after bestowing kanthi-diksha, Jivanji Maharaj carries on this discussion in order to remove the confused illusion about form and formlessness from the minds of devotees such as Gopaldas, Santdas, and Devdas. To make this clear to these devotees of Malwa, Jivanji Maharaj also recites a few shlokas --

_Sthaanam na yaanam na cha bindunaadam, roopam na rekhaa na cha dhaatuvargam,
Pushpam na gandham na phalam na chhaayaa, tasmai namo brahmaniranjanaay ||37||_ (To him who has no place and no going [no means of travel], no bindu, no naad, no form, no line, no group of elements, no flower, no scent, no fruit, and no shadow -- to that Niranjan Brahma, my salutations. -- 37)

_Adho na chodhvam na Shivo na Shakti, na naari pumaannaiva cha lingamoortih,
Kaalo na jeevo na guru na shishyah, tasmai namo brahmaniranjanaay ||38||_ (To him who is neither above nor below, neither Shiva nor Shakti, neither woman nor man, neither linga nor image, neither Time nor an individual soul, neither guru nor disciple -- to that Niranjan Brahma, my salutations. -- 38)

_Na paanchabhootam na cha saptasaagaram disho, na patraani na Meru-Mandaram,
Brahmaa na Rudro na cha Vishnuroopam, tasmai namo brahmaniranjanaay ||39||_ (To him who is not the five elements, not the seven seas, not the directions, not the leaves, not Mount Meru or Mandar, not Brahma, not Rudra, and not even Vishnu -- to that Niranjan Brahma, my salutations. -- 39)

What, then, are these teachings about the formless (nirakar) nature? The attributes of Parbrahma are: he is not white, not yellow, not dark, not blue, not red -- he has no colour at all; he is colourless. He is not Brahma, not Rudra, not Vishnu, not Indra, nor any god; not any rishi or sage; not a demon; not a country or a region; not the sky, not the earth, not the netherworld; he is no one's enemy nor anyone's friend; he has no joy and no grief; he is not born, nor does he pass through any other state (youth, middle age, or old age), nor does he die. Such a Parbrahma is known by the name Vasudev alone. He has no form; he is Niranjan (unstained) and Nirakar (formless). Then a natural question arises: what, then, is this "place" from which he is said to have appeared? To this we answer: whatever the mental disposition (vasana) of each devotee who worshipped Parbrahma at the time, such was the description they gave; each one saw Parbrahma according to whatever inclination (mansa -- wish or belief) was in their own mind.

What Jivanji Maharaj means to say here is this: without falling into confusion over questions like "What is Parbrahma like? To whom does he appear? What worship should be done? What mantra should be chanted?", and without getting entangled in the dispute over form and formlessness, one should, through pure character, constantly remember, contemplate, and meditate upon that all-powerful, glorious power which pervades the whole universe. His own devotees have only to sing his own qualities -- they should not fall into argument and debate.

Here, in one pada from Narsinh Mehta's "Haarmala" (the Garland), he sang --

_Sanyaasi vairaagi vismay paamyaa, vartyo jai jaikaar sarva dekhataan_ (Sannyasis and vairagis were struck with wonder; cries of victory rang out, in full view of all --)

When God gave the garland to Narsinh in front of all the devotees, seventeen sannyasis and vairagis (renunciants) were struck with amazement, and cries of jai-jaikar (victory) rang out, for it was in full view of everyone that God placed the garland around Narsinh Mehta's neck. And whatever devotion was in each one's heart, that is the form in which the compassionate Lord, kind to the humble, appeared to them. To Narsinh Mehta himself, God -- Madan Gopal -- came and embraced him again and again. At the Mukund ashram they saw God as Mukund; at the Keshav ashram, as Keshav; at the Narsingh ashram, as Narsingh; at the Madhav ashram, as Madhav; at the Brahma ashram, as Brahma-form; Shridhar saw him as a brahmachari; at the Vasudev ashram, as Vasudev; at the Shiva ashram, as Tripurari; at the Achyut ashram, as Achyut; at the Vishveshwar ashram, as Vishvambhar; at the Narayan ashram, as Narayan; at the Damodar ashram, as Damodar; Prasad Puri saw him in the form of Niranjan; Bhim saw him as Ram; the king's mother saw him as Chaturbhuj (four-armed); the queen saw him as beautiful, dark Shyam; the princess (Kunvar Bai) saw him as her grandfather; the protector of the world saw him as compassionate to the humble; the minister saw him in the form of universal dissolution; the king saw him in the form of Time (Kaal); the man of Brahma-knowledge saw him as the all-pervading form -- and thus everyone's doubt was dispelled, and that playful, charming, plume-crowned God embraced Narsinh Mehta by the neck.

In this pada, Narsinh Mehta shows that regarding Parbrahma Parmeshwar, one should stay above argument and above the question of form versus formlessness -- let anyone speak of whatever form they wish -- but in one's own personal life, one should worship according to whatever belief one holds faith in, or according to what a true Sadguru instructs (there are more false gurus in this world than true ones). On the matter of Parbrahma, Narsinh Mehta is entirely clear.

Jivanji Maharaj too says: this benevolent nature of Parbrahma is unlike anything else. Jivanji Maharaj says he is formless -- how, then, can the supreme Govind be said to have form? From the mythological story in which he took Hiranyakashipu onto his lap and tore him apart with his claws, he came to be given the name Narsingh -- but this cannot mean that the Supreme Lord actually possesses a form.

Here Jivanji Maharaj has explained one point with great depth and subtlety of meaning. The way the incarnations of Parbrahma and their deeds are outlined in the mythological narratives should not be used merely on the surface to judge or evaluate Parbrahma's deeds or life. We are not really concerned with either Hiranyakashipu or the Narsingh avatar as such -- rather, the lesson is to be drawn from the life of the devotee Prahlad. And, just as we have said earlier that God is affectionate toward his devotees (bhakta-vatsal), so was the devotee Prahlad protected -- this indeed is a source of great joy for devotees. Yet the lesson or essence that ought to be drawn from this episode has today been set aside, and the world has turned onto a wayward path. No one wishes to follow the path of the devotee-king Prahlad, or to give any real thought to anything at all. When we have become followers of a self-interested world, good thoughts simply do not arise in the mind; and even when good thoughts do come from outside, they are stopped right at the threshold of our own ears.

Just how much study the revered Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj must have made of the Niranjan Purana becomes apparent from these shlokas, 37 to 39, presented here. We cannot even imagine the depth with which the revered Jivanji Maharaj must have tried to understand the manner and practice of the followers of so many scriptures -- the Vedas, the Puranas, the Sahasranama, the Gita, the Bhagavat, the Ramayana, and so on. If so, we do not even have the capacity to understand all that he must have looked into. Let us, then, reflect a little with a truly far-reaching vision on these shlokas from the Niranjan Purana that this great Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj has presented, and let us appreciate the graciousness Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj has showered upon us. Shloka 37 states how far beyond the illusion (maya) of this world that Niranjan Brahma is: that Niranjan Brahma needs no place, and no vehicle for going anywhere, nor does he have any nada-bindu (sound-point). Let us here discuss nada-bindu. Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, through very deep investigation, having, at the end of all kinds of striving, experienced the complete truth in which God's true essence resides, granted us the devotion of ratankaar [the constant inner repetition of the Name] and thereby brought about our welfare -- let us remember this kindness.

The Nadabindu Upanishad is an Upanishad of that name belonging to the Rig Veda branch. Nadabindu means the syllable Om. Nadabindu is the point (bindu) at which one fixes one's attention on the inner sound (nada). This Upanishad follows the model of the Chulika Upanishad. The Nadabindu Upanishad is one of the Upanishads of the Yoga group; it is composed in verse. Sadguru Kabirji, too, dismissed the nada-bindu [as insufficient by itself]. He has a pada on this in the Kalyan raga.

(Raga Kalyan, Granth 79, page 117.)

_Tum niranjan tum niranjan, tum niranjan raaya,
Taheru roop naanhi rekh naanhi, mudraa naanhi na maayaa. (tek)_

_Taahe naad naanhi bund naanhi, kaal naanhi kaayaa,
Ravi shashi doou eke naanhi, taa dan na Raam Raaya ||1||_

_Taa din samudra naanhi ne shikhar naanhi, dharani naanhi naan gaganaa,
Chaar jug brahmaand naanhi, paavak naanhi na pavanaa ||2||_

_Taa din devata naanhi ne dev naanhi, paanti naanhi ne poojaa naanhi,
Abe tabe tumhi ho swami, aur naanhi naa doojaa koi ||3||_

_Rig jajur aur saam atharved, bidyaa naanhi ne vaakun karani,
Teri teri gat tuhi jaane, daas Kabir tum sharan ||4||_

(O Lord, you are niranjan -- free of any stain or illusion -- you are the King of Niranjan itself. You have no form, no outline or shape or kind whatsoever; no facial form and no attachment to maya. You have no nada, nor any bindu that fixes upon the nada, nor any Om-ness; nor do you have Time or a body. On that day neither the sun nor the moon existed, nor did King Ram exist on that day; there was neither ocean nor mountain, neither earth nor sky. The four yugas and the cosmos itself did not exist; there was no fire, no wind; there was no deity and no god; there was no leaf, no flower, no worship or discussion of worship. In that time, and in this present time too, O Lord, you alone are the master -- there is no other besides you. There was no learning of the Rig, Yajur, Sama, or Atharva Vedas, nor any of the ritual acts prescribed in those Vedas. Only you yourself can know your own way and manner. Kabir, your servant, has come to your shelter.)

The sense contained in the words "nad" and "bund" is not something ordinarily understood, and so the common mass of people fall into error over it. They take the deeper meaning of "nad" to refer to the sentiment of Hari-kirtan (singing God's praise); or they take "nad" to mean divine inspiration, the voice of the inner self; or they understand it as the Guru's teaching. A similar confusion arises with the word "bund" as well -- it is taken to mean the hereditary son and successor of the Guru. We ourselves have held this same misunderstanding. The Vaishnav Nana Parekh, in writing anew an account of the departure to the divine abode -- in order to supply the burnt-away latter portion of the Samagam -- wrote, in the Udadharma-Panchratnamala, third edition, page 329, that Vaishnav Jivandasji said, "Dharma belongs to nad." Here he used this word "nad" because he was drawn to it. The intent behind using this word "nad" was that the basis for carrying dharma forward lies with one who properly understands the Guru's teaching -- such a person is fit to carry dharma forward. Further, people also take the meaning of "bund" to be that dharma does not belong by bund -- that is, it should not be understood that only the Guru's literal son can carry dharma forward. But nad-bund is, in fact, an entirely different matter. The word "bund" is a corrupted form of "bindu" -- "bund" is a word used, mistakenly, in place of "bindu." Nad-bund is, in fact, a term from the path of yoga, referring to Omkar. So it is not possible that Jivanji Maharaj -- who had made a complete study of all the paths of the world -- would use such a word as "nad" [in that confused, lineage-related sense] at his final hour. He himself has said in his own sakhi --

_Garbhadhyaan chinho nahi, kare Harijansun vivaad,
Ant bhaandivaado Jivana, kaha raachyo anahad naad ||4||_ (Garbhavali -- 44) (One who follows the path of yoga, but fails to understand the innermost meaning of the ratankaar of Ram's Name -- the divine essence dwelling within one's own soul -- and instead picks a quarrel, clutching at the tail-end of Omkar as a yogi, with devotees who practise devotion through the constant repetition [ratankaar] of Ram's Name: your fate in the end will be like that of a potter in a potter's quarter, firing pots in his kiln -- you too will have to be roasted in the fire of the womb, through the eighty-four lakh species of birth. So why do you climb onto the addiction of the unstruck sound [anahad nad] and remain absorbed in it? Better, instead, to follow the constant repetition of Ram's Name; walking the path of devotion will bring about your welfare.)

A great soul who was giving us such understanding would himself never use the word "nad" in that mistaken sense; but because we failed to grasp the true meaning of the word "nad," we -- from Nana Parekh down to the present day -- have been caught in a major error. Yet, from the moment we come to true understanding, we ought to correct our mistake. The devotees of Surat district had printed a book, for singing bhajan-kirtan just as we do, under the title "Ramkabir." But when a second edition was to be printed, a certain gentleman -- who, like us, had fallen into misunderstanding -- insisted on changing this title to "Nad Brahma" instead. This gentleman, who insisted on the change, once met me at Puniyad and told me that he had made a point of having the name "Nad Brahma" given to the book. I did not argue with him. But the kirtan-bhakti we perform, and the sound we raise in our kirtans through kaansi, mridang and narghan (cymbals, drum, and small kettledrums) -- that sound should not be called "nad." It is, rather, the voice of loving devotion born of the ceaseless repetition (ratankaar) of Ram's Name, rising up from within the soul. That sound is not nad; it is the resounding voice (nirghosh) that arises from the sound of the kaansi, mridang and so on, produced by a loving devotee wholly absorbed in devotion to Hari. We sing thus --

_Nand aangane nirghosh vaage, paanch shabdano poore naad._ (In the courtyard of Nand [Krishna's father], the sacred sound resounds -- the fullness of the five-fold sound.)

Thus, in this context, the word "nad" applies to our kirtan-bhakti; in that kirtan, as many as five kinds of sound come together, and so in this sense we do accept the word "nad." But not "Nad Brahma" -- rather, a word like "nad-bhakti" or "nad-kirtan" would be fitting for us; but for our faith, the word "nad-dharma" is not acceptable. In the five-fold sound, all five senses become immersed and drenched, absorbed in one single love.

God possesses the quality of niranjan-ness (being free of any stain); yet in Vraj Bhoomi there is the garden of Vrishbhanuji [Radha's father]. There is a village there named after a sakhi (companion) called Kamai; Shri Radha-Krishna used to visit her home. Near there is Ajnokhri, where there is Anjankund -- a pond where Shri Krishna applied anjan (kohl) to Radhaji's eyes. Referring to this, someone has written --

_Dhanyaa Gokulakanyaa vayamiha manyaamahe jagati,
Yaasaam nayanasaroje ajjaneebhooto niranjano vasati,
Suranjano'bhoot niranjanah saakshaat ||2||_ (I consider the gopa-maidens blessed in this world, in whose lotus eyes the very Niranjan [Krishna, the unstained one] himself has become anjan [the mark] and dwells as Suranjan -- that is, in whose eyes Shri Krishna resides, day and night. -- 2)

Such was the prem-lakshana bhakti (devotion characterised by pure love) of the gopis, that even one who is anjan-rahit (free of any mark) could become anjan-vaalo (bearing the mark). Adhyaruji, too, says --

_Khele khele jo rang Gopal niranjan anjanvaan shareero._ (Even though God is niranjan and nirakar [formless], for the sake of the gopis he became a body bearing form and plays with them -- such is that Gopal Krishna.)

Thus Jivanji Maharaj inspires us to practise this same kind of prem-lakshana devotion that the gopis had. "If one has form, fire cannot save him" -- this eternal, true statement Jivanji Maharaj repeated many times in the Samagam, and its meaning is very deep. Even if you reflect and meditate on this small sentence, a great deal of truth will become clear. In India the festival of Holi is celebrated, but we have killed the greatness that lies behind this festival.

According to one Puranic story, a demon named Hiranyakashipu became king, and, intoxicated by power, began to work destruction instead of the welfare of his subjects. Once he gained power, he began to fly high with pride, as though no one else could be more powerful than he; he even proclaimed himself to be God, and commanded his subjects to praise and worship him. But his son, though only a small child in years, turned out to be wise and just. The people could not oppose Hiranyakashipu's command, and, with heavy hearts, submitted to him, each thinking only of their own safety; out of a craving for momentary pleasure, they accepted the falsehood. Only his own son opposed his father's command. Sufferings came upon him, and he had to pass through many trials; a reign of threat and intimidation began, but still he would not yield. In the end, it was decided that he should be burned to death, to remove the threat once and for all. His beloved, favoured sister, Holika, had received a boon that she could never be burned, however fierce the fire; so it was arranged that she would sit with Prahlad on her lap while a fire was lit -- but Prahlad survived.

There are many festivals celebrated, of which four are principal: Shravan-Rakshabandhan for Brahmins; second, Dashera for Kshatriyas; third, Deepavali for Vaishyas; and fourth, Holi for Shudras.
